THE McGILL DAILY, TWO ISSUES: 2 MARCH 1938 AND 9 OCTOBER 1941
A ski party navigating by the camp, and Hupfield at Otoreke a year earlier than the yearbook

Found 2026-09-07 by the whole-corpus sweep of 9,890 McGill student publication
items under p_479. Term counts run rather than assumed: 1938 issue Kanawana 1,
Otoreke 0; 1941 issue Otoreke 1, Kanawana 0.

Note how the second was found. "Hupfield" returns ZERO in the 1941 text: the
paper broke it across a line as "Mr. Hup- field". The sweep matched on
"Otoreke". A name search would have missed this document entirely, which is a
general caution for OCR of narrow newspaper columns.

===============================================================================
1. 2 MARCH 1938 — "LOST SKIERS FIND TRAILS"
===============================================================================

READ THE WHOLE ARTICLE BEFORE USING IT. The Kanawana sentence, taken alone,
reads as though a student conference were being held at the camp. IT WAS NOT.
The conference was at Madame Hébert's "Laurentide Home" on the shores of Lac
Guindon, about three miles up the lumber trail from Shawbridge. Kanawana enters
only as a landmark that lost skiers recognised. This was misread on first
sight here and corrected by reading the article, which is the whole reason for
transcribing it in full.

  "LOST SKIERS FIND TRAILS

  Free to explore all the trails in the St. Sauveur-Shawbridge district, but
  only feeling secure when at the bottom of Hill 70, the members of the S.C.M.
  ski conference arrived in Montreal last night after spending the week-end
  recess at Lac Guindon. Led by Dr. Fred Howes, discussion during the
  conference periods centred about the main theme 'Freedom and Security.'

  Among the 42 students attending the ski conference were five co-eds from
  Macdonald College, and Holley Fletcher, student at the University of Vermont.
  The party arrived at Lac Guindon, which is about three miles up the lumber
  trail from Shawbridge, in time for lunch on Saturday. About half the party
  left on Sunday night in time for the early train, but the remainder either
  stayed at Lac Guindon during Monday, or skied along trails in the vicinity
  until the 6.05 train from Shawbridge.

  VISIT HILL 70. The week-end was spent at Madame Hebert's 'Laurentide Home,'
  on the shores of Lac Guindon. During the daytime, the programme consisted
  chiefly of skiing. On Saturday most of the 42 present skied along the Douglas
  Trail, emerging from the woods at the top of Hill 70, where the rest of the
  afternoon was spent. The conference proper began on Saturday evening when
  Neil Morrison, S.C.M. secretary, gave a short talk on 'The Present
  Situation,' and showed how students everywhere are beginning to take a more
  active part in the life of the society in which they live. After a short
  question period, Dr. Howes gave the first short address on the topic 'Freedom
  and Security.' On Sunday morning a short service was held led by Ivor
  Williams. [...] The remainder of the morning was occupied by a talk by Dr.
  Howes.

  SKIING PARTY LOST. During Sunday afternoon, one skiing party got itself into
  such a predicament that at one time each of its nine members was pointing to
  a different direction for return. WHEN THEY NEARED KAMP KANAWANA THEY WERE
  FINALLY LED BACK SAFELY UNDER THE DIRECTION OF TWO OLD KANAWANIANS IN THE
  PARTY, only half an hour too late for supper.

  The conference proper was brought to a close on Sunday evening, when Dr.
  Howes finished his remarks. Monday was devoted wholly to skiing, one party
  managing to get itself lost on the snow-silted Johannsen-West trail, and only
  arriving at St. Margaret's with 15 minutes to go before the departure of the
  one and only evening train."

WHAT IT ACTUALLY GIVES.

(a) "TWO OLD KANAWANIANS", IN PRINT, IN 1938, IN SOMEBODY ELSE'S NEWSPAPER.
    The wiki has "Kanawanian" as a term of belonging from the camp's own
    literature -- the 1964 annual report's "Forty thousand boys have earned the
    title 'Kanawanian'", the 1980 Knights of Kanawana charter, the Order of
    Owens citation, and a counsellor's "We are all Kanawanians" of 2004-05. All
    of those are the institution using its own word. This is a student
    newspaper using it in passing about two men in a ski party, with no gloss,
    twenty-six years before the earliest dated instance held here. A word used
    without explanation in an outside publication is in general currency, which
    is a different and stronger claim than a camp branding its alumni.

(b) THE CAMP AS A WINTER LANDMARK. Nine lost skiers in the St-Sauveur-Shawbridge
    trail network in March 1938 knew where they were when they came in sight of
    Kanawana, and two men who had been campers there could navigate home from
    it. That says the site was known, recognisable and passable in deep winter,
    and that the trail country the camp sits in was being skied through by
    Montreal students between the wars.

(c) WHAT IT DOES NOT GIVE, STATED SO NOBODY LATER READS IT BACK IN. No winter
    programme at Kanawana. No use of the camp's buildings. The party was at Lac
    Guindon and merely passed near.

(d) The S.C.M. connection is worth noting beside the Sir George material found
    the same day: Murray B. Shantz was President of the S.C.M. at Sir George in
    1943 and George N. Barker President of its Group in 1941-42. The same
    movement, in the same years, running ski conferences in the same district.

===============================================================================
2. 9 OCTOBER 1941 — "RE-MODELLED PIT RE-OPENS"
===============================================================================

  "The Pit, co-operative cafeteria in the basement of Strathcona Hall, will
  present a new appearance and atmosphere to those students who took advantage
  of its facilities in past years. THERE IS AN ENTIRELY NEW STAFF UNDER THE
  MANAGEMENT OF MR. HUP-FIELD, DIRECTOR OF THE Y.M.C.A. CAMP OTOREKE, AND
  FOURTH YEAR ARTS STUDENT. Acting in the capacity of new chef is Mother Mac,
  who, with the co-operation of the staff, has promised to attempt fulfilling
  the Pit's new policy, that of serving good food in the home-cooked manner, at
  prices in keeping with the new war-time economy. The Pit has been renovated
  in many respects. The new concrete floor has been painted red, the walls
  sport a new colour combination, and the windows have been adorned with
  fluffy, white curtains. Designed as further attractions for the students are
  new signs around the walls, a new pop-cooler, and a new nickelodeon to supply
  background music."

WHY THIS MATTERS. Earlier the same day this project corrected
wiki/site/camp-otoreke.md, which had concluded that Ron Hupfield "does not
appear on the Montreal staff at all until 1947 and is never placed at Otoreke
by any source held here," using his graduating entry in Sir George Williams
College's 1942 yearbook. THIS IS A SECOND, INDEPENDENT SOURCE FROM A DIFFERENT
INSTITUTION, AND IT IS EARLIER: October 1941, a McGill student newspaper, in a
story that has nothing to do with camps and no reason to flatter him. He is
"director of the Y.M.C.A. Camp Otoreke" as a plain identifying fact about the
man running the cafeteria.

It also puts flesh on "Mgr. Strathcona Hall, '41 & '42" from the yearbook: what
he managed there was The Pit, the co-operative cafeteria in the basement, and
he took it over with an entirely new staff at the start of the 1941-42 session.

ONE THING NOT SMOOTHED OVER. The Daily calls him a "fourth year Arts student"
without naming a college, and its readers were McGill's. The Sir George
yearbook has him graduating in Arts from SIR GEORGE in 1942, which fits a
fourth year in October 1941. The likeliest reading is that a Sir George student
managed the McGill YMCA's cafeteria and the Daily did not think the distinction
worth making -- which would itself be a fact about how porous the two YMCA
institutions were. But the article does not say so and this is left open.

A TRAP, RECORDED BECAUSE THIS ARTICLE HAS ONE ALREADY. "Mother Mac" here is the
Pit's new chef in Montreal in 1941. She is NOT "Mr. Mac", Clarence J.
McGerrigle, Otoreke's long-serving director. camp-otoreke.md already carries one
warning of this kind, about a V. McAdam of the Boys Clubs of Canada whom a
careless OCR read would turn into "Mr. Mac".
